Imagine a very eager student changing their answers to fit every little detail of practice questions, even noise. They fit practice data beautifully but fail on new questions. Our computer models can do this too, learning too much noise. We give the model a 'leash' to keep its answers sensible.

We add a penalty for large 'weights' – the numbers the model learns. Ridge regression uses a soft leash: it gently pulls all weights smaller, but never to zero. LASSO regression uses a sharp leash: it can pull some weights exactly to zero, turning off unhelpful features.

Let's see an example. If a model's best 'weight' for a feature is 3 without a penalty. Ridge, with a penalty, will shrink it, maybe to 1 or 0.3, but always keeps it positive. LASSO, however, with a strong enough penalty, can make that weight exactly zero, completely removing that feature.

For your exam, remember that Ridge never makes weights exactly zero; LASSO can. Both add penalties to stop models from learning noise and overfitting. We choose the right 'leash strength', called lambda, by finding what works best on new data. Great job learning this complex idea!
